document.title: The Taliban - Who Knows What the Movement Means?
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
document.note: [Confidential] Discusses the suspected origins, goals and sponsors of the Taliban, which now controls most of Kandahar province. The Rabbani/Masoud government is worried by the Taliban's rapid growth. The Taliban offer hope to war-weary Afghans disgusted with national leaders' failure to compromise.

events.description: Taliban movement begins in Kandahar to open roads and end banditry.
Reported mid-September Jalalabad meetings of Rabbani, Sayyaf and others deciding to back the movement, following Fazlur Rahman's suggestion.
Taliban rose to prominence as Babar's relief convoy attempted to enter Afghanistan; fighting with HIG and Ittehad commanders.
Haji Mohammed Ghaus interview criticizing Pakistan over the convoy.
Maulawi Terakhel tells the Peshawar principal officer he rejected leadership of the Kandahari Taliban.
Maulawi Terakhel's summer 1979 attack on Kabul airport precipitated evacuation of American dependents.
US Embassy Islamabad cable on the Taliban sent.
US Embassy Islamabad cable assessing the Taliban's origins, sponsors, and likely beneficiaries.
Mid-September meetings in Jalalabad between Rabbani, Sayyaf and others, allegedly deciding to launch the Taliban movement following Fazlur Rahman's suggestion.
Mohammad Omar and Fazlur Rahman reportedly requested and received Rabbani's permission in Jalalabad to clean up the Chaman-Kandahar highway.
Haji Mohammed Ghaus interviewed in Spin Boldak, criticizing Pakistan over the truck convoy and Karachi transit bottlenecks.
Maulawi Terakhel met the Peshawar principal officer and said he had rejected leadership of the Kandahari Taliban.
Maulawi Terakhel's attack on Kabul airport prompted evacuation of American dependents from Kabul.
SCC dispatched a delegation led by Hasmatullah Mojadeddi to Quetta to assess the Taliban.
Maulawi Terakhel's summer 1979 attack on Kabul airport precipitated the evacuation of American dependents from Kabul.
Maulawi Terakhel met US political officer and said he had rejected leadership of the Kandahari Taliban.
Nangarhar Shura dispatched an additional 400 men to the Torkham border to guard against disturbances.
US Embassy Islamabad sent cable 11247 on the Taliban to Washington.
Taliban movement began in Kandahar province to open roads and end banditry.
Taliban rose to prominence in late September as Babar's relief convoy attempted to enter Afghanistan.
Haji Mohammed Ghaus interview in Spin Boldak criticizing Pakistan over the convoy.
US Embassy Islamabad cable on Taliban drafted by Consulate Peshawar.

key_claims: The origins, goals and sponsors of the Taliban remain unclear even to well-informed Afghans.
Many observers believe the movement was initially sponsored by Pakistan, though most Afghans say Islamabad no longer controls it.
JUI leader Fazlur Rahman is described as an active supporter of the Taliban.
Rabbani allegedly approved the Taliban's highway clean-up at Jalalabad meetings; Ismael Khan said Rabbani funded the group.
Mullah Naqib, a Jamiat commander, was coopted by or supports the Taliban in Kandahar.
The Taliban draw core and leaders from the old anti-Soviet Taliban group and enjoy bazaari and popular support.
Party leaders Hekmatyar and Rabbani are worried by Taliban growth and seek to coopt them.
Taliban successes in Ghazni and Zabul depended more on bribing commanders than on fighting.
Taliban are not acting to the exclusive benefit of any established vested interest.
Strong Afghan popular support for the Taliban reflects frustration with party leaders and a desire for peace and stability.
Taliban might help bring party leaders (Hekmatyar, Khalis, Rabbani, Sayyaf) together against a common threat.
Taliban's local success may revive non-partisan Kandahari traditionalists/royalists or compromise candidates like Nabi Mohammadi.
Some contacts feared the OIC, Sudan-based extremists, or Pakistani fundamentalists could sabotage the UN peace process.
Taliban origins and sponsorship remain an enigma, with conflicting reports.
